runs.text: tra couſa, ou declarar & diſtinguir algũa couſa.

lines.note: Tra completes ou-tra from the preceding page's Iyfiraqi entry. The gloss continues with explaining and distinguishing a matter; this is running text, not a second catchword.
Iyfucume means instructing someone thoroughly by speech. The visible t in Inſtruir corrects OCR Inſiruir without altering the historical typography.
De palaura specifies oral instruction, completing the preceding gloss. It is not a separate headword or marginal note.
Iyfuraxi means spreading a report or making something known. The Portuguese alternative diuulgar begins here and continues below.
The example says that the person spread the report that he was going to Kumano. Iy furaite is a historical -aite form, not a damaged modern -ashite ending.
Cuniuo vttatta completes the example of departing from the province or realm. The Portuguese begins the same account of leaving while putting a report into circulation.

runs.text: fama que hia em romaria a Cumano.

lines.note: The circulated report was that he was going on pilgrimage to Cumano. Cumano is a Japanese place name embedded in Portuguese and is printed in the italic explanatory context.

runs.text: Hũa pàſinha com que metẽ o arroz nas

lines.note: Iygai names the small scoop used to put rice into bowls, not a speaking compound. Second-pass enlargement confirms the distinct grave accent over a in pàſinha; it is restored rather than flattening the word to an unaccented form.
Eſcudelas supplies the bowls receiving the rice and completes the scoop definition. The short physical row is preserved.
Iymorai, alternatively meibo, is an eyelid stye. The Portuguese historical word Terçor is retained as printed, with olhos divided across the line break.
Iymoraiga deqita means that a stye has developed. Naceo me begins the Portuguese rendering from the affected speaker's point of view.
Completes the statement that a stye appeared in the eyes. The historical terçor is repeated, supporting the same reading in the headword gloss.
Iynarauaxi concerns customary or transmitted sayings. The Portuguese pairs dizer perdedução with passing into common talk below; the compact printed perdedução is retained.
Correr em pratica completes the customary-report gloss. The example begins with Benkei being spoken of as an oni or a kami, with ca- continuing below.

Mino completes the divided ca-mino spelling, interpreted together as kami no: people customarily spoke of Benkei as like an oni or kami. The historical iy narauaita form is retained, and He commũ begins its translation.

runs.text: dizer dos homẽs que Benquei era como diabo,

lines.note: The Portuguese says that it is a common saying among people that Benquei was like a devil. Benquei is the name as printed within Portuguese, distinct from Benqeiuo in the Japanese example.
Ou Cami completes the comparison with a kami. Cami is a Japanese religious term embedded in the Portuguese clause and is not translated into a different canonical word.
Iynaxi is saying or representing something in a particular manner. The following rows explain that the manner intensifies or strengthens its characterization.

runs.text: que encarece, & confirma as couſas em boa, ou

lines.note: The manner of speaking heightens and confirms matters, either favourably or unfavourably. The favourable alternative begins em boa and continues into parte by coordination.
Em mà parte completes the unfavourable alternative. The grave accent on mà is preserved rather than normalized to modern má.
Iynobe means extending or delaying something through words. The Portuguese dilatar is retained without narrowing it to a modern paraphrase unsupported by an example.
Iynoboxe concerns sending word upward to the capital. The capital I corrects OCR long s; the historical ſuru principal part belongs to nobose.
Miaco completes the destination, the capital, in the Portuguese explanation. The Japanese place term is printed in italic here.
Iyo iyo means more and more or increasingly. The first printed letter is a low, damaged i-like form; lowercase iyo is retained here rather than importing NINJAL-style headword capitalization.
Iyo yacana describes something clear and distinct. The visible cl sequence in clara replaces the OCR d; the printed separation in the Japanese form is preserved.
Iyoyacani is the adverbial form, explained by Qirarito and maguiremonǒ, without indistinctness. The final caron on ǒ is visible; Cla continues below without a printed hyphen.
Ra completes clara and the adverbial Portuguese gloss says clearly and distinctly. The printed st sequence is not globally recast as long s.
Iyqicaxe means telling something to another person or making that person hear it. The historical ſuru form is retained as part of the verb paradigm.
Iytate begins an extended entry for speaking of someone in detail, well or ill. The initial is capital I, not the OCR lowercase l.

runs.text: guem contando miudamente ſuas virtudes, ou

lines.note: The account enumerates someone's virtues or, as completed below, vices. This specifies the evaluative detail involved in Iytate.
The negative example speaks at length against another person's name or reputation. The physical ending iyta- belongs to iytatçuru continued below, not a separate verb.
Tçuru completes iytatçuru. The Portuguese translates the example as speaking ill of someone extensively, confirming the reputational sense.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Dizer algũa couſa relatandoa miu-

lines.note: A further sense is relating a matter in detail. The attached pronoun in relatandoa is preserved as printed, with miudamente divided below.
Dǒriuo iytatçuru means setting out a reason or argument. The Portuguese Are- begins the corresponding act of reasoning across the row boundary.

runs.text: zoar bem, ou dar rezão dalgũa couſa miu-

lines.note: Completes Are-zoar and adds giving an account of something in detail. Printed rezão is retained rather than standardized to razão.
Damente completes miudamente, emphasizing detailed explanation. It is a short continuation of the argument example.

runs.text: O falar, ou relatar algũa couſa miuda-

lines.note: The separate noun Iytate is detailed speaking or narration. The scan shows y, not the OCR v in Ivtate; the headword is distinct from the preceding verb paradigm.
After completing miudamente, the entry adds a theatrical sense: a prologue or introductory representation. The second noun continues below.

runs.text: ção que ſe faz no principio dalgum auto, ou

lines.note: The representation occurs at the beginning of an auto or dramatic piece. This begins an account of an introductory speech, not a new dictionary entry.

runs.text: hiſtoria que ſe repreſenta, dando noticia do que

lines.note: The prologue informs the audience about the story being represented. The relative clause continues into what is to be performed below.
Completes the prologue's task of explaining what is to be performed. The compact hade spelling is preserved rather than separated into modern words.
Iytçume means overcoming or cornering someone by argument. The Portuguese conuencer introduces the verbal means completed below.
Palauras and disputando specify words or disputation as the means of overcoming the other person. This completes the argumentative sense.
Iytçuqe means ordering or telling someone to do something. The Portuguese alguem is divided at the line end.
Guem completes alguem, and mandando lhe clarifies that the telling is an instruction or command. The printed separated pronoun is preserved.
Iytçutaye means transmitting a saying or receiving it through tradition. Tra begins tradição below; no terminal hyphen is visible in the native crop.
The fragment dição completes tradição, the means of transmission. This is the final body row of column 1 and not page furniture.
Iytçuzzuqe means continuing to speak or converse. The pale initial I and damaged r of uru are read from their surviving strokes and the verb paradigm, correcting OCR ſytçuzzuqe, ufu.
Comagomato fitotoqi bacari begins an example of speaking in detail for about one interval of time. The final iytçuz- continues the same verb below.
Completes the concessive verbal form and cites Fox., book 2. The italic abbreviation is visibly Lib., not OCR Lih.; Co begins the Portuguese translation without a terminal hyphen.

runs.text: mo hũa hora foi continuando a pratica miuda-

lines.note: Completes Como and describes continuing the detailed conversation for about an hour. Hũa is abraded, especially the u and its mark; the surviving traces and hour construction support this reading rather than OCR ha.
Mente completes miudamente, the detailed manner of conversation. This is the last row of the cited example.
Iytodome means stopping or detaining someone through words. The Portuguese deter supplies the restraining sense.
Iyvataxi means telling or delivering a message. The recipient follows on the next short row.
A outro completes the recipient, another person. This is a continuation of delivering a message, not an independent entry.
Iyvocuri means sending word or having something told. The final utta is the printed past principal part, with doubled t retained.
Iyvoqi means leaving something said or leaving instructions. The initial is capital I, not OCR long s, and the oita past form is retained.
Iyvouari means finishing what one is saying. The capital I corrects OCR long s; the compound contains owaru rather than an unrelated beginning in s.
Iyvôxe means imputing something to another person. The pale initial I is restored from its residual stroke and the surrounding iy- series; the circumflex on ô is preserved.
Fitoni togauo iyvôſuru means imputing a fault to a person. Enlargement shows the bottom-joined u of the object particle uo, not OCR n; this corrects togano without emending a genuine printed anomaly.
Gum completes algum, and the translation explicitly imputes a crime to someone. This supplies the intended accusation sense without licensing alteration of the Japanese example.
Iyyari means sending word or having a matter communicated. The double y belongs to the printed compound and is not simplified.

runs.text: O comporem algũs de boca verſos, ou

lines.note: Iyzute denotes composing verses orally. The initial capital I corrects OCR long s; the following lines describe improvisation and continuation by another participant.

runs.text: cantigas derepente, ou o continuar alguem com

lines.note: The gloss covers spontaneous songs and a person continuing a verse. The compact derepente spelling remains as printed.

runs.text: a parte do verſo que outro começou. ¶

lines.note: A participant adds the part of a verse begun by another person. Iy- starts the accompanying example across the line break.
Iyzuteuo ſuru means composing verses in that manner. This closes the iy- section before the separate I ANTES DO Z heading.

runs.text: Interjeição de exhortar. i, eia. Vt,

lines.note: IZa is an exhortation, glossed with Portuguese eia. The enlarged I was omitted from the OCR text; Za follows it on the same physical line. The scan supports exhortar and eia rather than echortar and cia.
Iza ite qicǒ urges going and listening, matching Eia indo ouçamos. The t in ite and the middle of Mon. are abraded; the surviving traces support the retained reading and citation label.
Izaiza repeats the exhortation, glossed as eia or orasus. The repetitive Japanese form is preserved rather than reduced to the preceding headword.
Izanai means leading or guiding someone. The marked-vowel principal parts are retained as printed despite the light impression of their accents.

runs.text: Aleijado que anda com as mãos pol-

lines.note: Izari is described in the source as a person with impaired mobility who moves using the hands. The scan supports Aleijado and com, not OCR Aeijado and cont; the historical descriptive wording is preserved.
Lo chão completes pollo chão, along the ground. It describes the manner of movement rather than introducing another term.
Izaſa names a plant compared with low little canes. The botanical gloss alone does not justify adding a modern species identification.
Izaſaraba is an exhortative expression, again glossed orasus. The abbreviated interject. is apparatus and remains unexpanded.

runs.text: Peſſoa que tem o ſono leue, ou ouue lo-

lines.note: Izatoi describes a light sleeper or someone who quickly hears a noise. The final lo- continues logo below.

runs.text: go qualquer eſtrondo inda que durma. No Ca

lines.note: The person hears a disturbance even while asleep. No Ca begins the regional label Cami, physically divided without a terminal hyphen.
Mi completes Cami; the dictionary says Yozatoi is used there. Both the divided regional name and Yozatoi occur within this Portuguese usage statement, unlike a standalone Japanese example.
Izatô is the adverb alert or wakefully. Izatô gozare is the exhortation to remain alert; the circumflex is kept as printed.

runs.text: Eſtejão todos álerta, ou não durmão profun-

lines.note: The example is translated as everyone remaining alert or not sleeping deeply. The scan supports todos and an accented álerta, correcting OCR todas dlerta.
Damente completes profundamente, the depth of sleep being discouraged. This belongs to the alertness example.
Izaya is another exhortative interjection. The pale initial I is retained from its surviving stroke, while the abbreviated interjection label remains unexpanded.

Izayoino tçuqi is the sixteenth-night moon, explained as the moon of the night of day sixteen. The scan supports possessive no rather than OCR uo, and consonantal I in Iǔrocunichino rather than long s.
Tçuqi completes the explanatory Japanese phrase. The Portuguese is Lũa, moon, not OCR Lũs, and specifies the night of the sixteenth day.
Izzuco means where and is marked P. for poetic usage. Here the P. introduces the explanation and is printed in italic, unlike some terminal upright usage labels.
Izzucu means where or in what place. Izzu- begins the example Izzucu mademo continued below.
Izzucu mademo is glossed as in every place. The printed word division cu mademo reflects the physical continuation and is not merged into the previous row.
Izzucumo receives Idem, referring to the preceding everywhere expression. It is an independent headword despite the one-word Portuguese gloss.
Izzucunimo also refers back with Idem to the same everywhere sense. The ni element is retained as part of this distinct headword.
Izzucuno can express which or from where. The example begins the question about a person's place of origin across the line break.
Izzucuno fitoca asks what place the person is from. De donde ſois gives the direct Portuguese equivalent; both question marks are retained.
Izzumi is a spring or fountain, glossed fonte. Its double z is retained rather than modernized to the current romanization.
Izzure means whichever, with Izzureca asking which. The final Portuguese word is Qual? with a question mark, not the OCR Quaſ-; the following Izzuremo is a separate catchword.
The catchword anticipates Izzuremo at the top of f281. The extra OCR l was part of the right rule, not additional text.
